claim: He never wrote a book. Everything we have was taken down by a student, Arrian.
evidence: whatever I heard him say, the same I attempted to write down in his own words as nearly as possible
author: Arrian
caveat: Arrian's word for how faithful the notes are; scholars still debate how much is Arrian's style.
use_in: Part 1 hook: the most quoted Stoic never wrote anything

claim: Arrian says the notes were published without his consent or knowledge.
evidence: I do not know how they fell into the hands of the public, without either my consent or my knowledge
author: Arrian

claim: He was enslaved in Rome. His owner was Epaphroditus, a freedman of the emperor Nero.
evidence: he was a slave in Rome, and his master was Epaphroditus, a profligate freedman of the emperor Nero
author: George Long (1877)
caveat: Long's summary; Epictetus names Epaphroditus himself in Discourses 1.19 and 1.26.

claim: Epictetus mentions his old owner by name and mocks how he fawned over a shoemaker he'd once sold.
evidence: Epaphroditus had a shoemaker whom he sold because he was good for nothing
author: Epictetus

claim: The famous story that his master broke his leg is doubtful. The older commentator Simplicius says he was weak and lame from an early age.
evidence: There is a story that the master broke his slave's leg by torturing him; but it is better to trust to the evidence of Simplicius
author: George Long (1877)
caveat: Both stories are ancient: the leg-breaking one comes from Celsus via Origen (Contra Celsum 7.53), not yet checked here. Say 'one story says', never state it as fact.

claim: He called himself 'a lame old man'.
evidence: what else can I do, a lame old man, than sing hymns to God
author: Epictetus

claim: He studied under the Stoic teacher Musonius Rufus.
evidence: Musonius Rufus, in order to try me, used to say
author: Epictetus

claim: His teacher Rufus judged a lecture had failed if the students only praised it.
evidence: If you have leisure to praise me, I am speaking to no purpose
author: Epictetus quoting Musonius Rufus
caveat: Rufus's words as Epictetus remembered them.

claim: Rufus deliberately tried to put students off, to see who would come back.
evidence: Rufus generally attempted to discourage (his pupils), and he used this method as a test
author: Epictetus

claim: When the emperor Domitian expelled philosophers from Rome, Epictetus moved to Nicopolis in Greece.
evidence: the philosopher Epictetus also withdrew from Rome to Nicopolis because of that senatorial decree
author: Aulus Gellius
licence: Public domain translation (Rolfe 1927); Perseus encoding CC BY-SA 4.0, credit Perseus
caveat: Gellius gives no year. Long and Rolfe say AD 89; modern accounts usually say about AD 93-95. Say 'under Domitian', not a year.

claim: At Nicopolis he opened a school and taught until he was old.
evidence: Epictetus opened a school or lecture room at Nicopolis, where he taught till he was an old man
author: George Long (1877)

claim: He never married, but late in life took in a baby a friend was going to abandon, and raised it.
evidence: Epictetus took the child and brought it up
author: George Long (1877)
tier: late ancient testimony via 19th c. scholar
caveat: Long relays Simplicius (6th c. AD), writing centuries later. Say 'an ancient commentator records'.
use_in: Appreciation post; not a hurt post

claim: Arrian's notes once filled eight books; only four survive.
evidence: These discourses formed eight books, but only four are extant
author: George Long (1877)
caveat: Count comes from Photius (9th c.); Long himself notes Photius may not have seen the books.

claim: The Enchiridion ('handbook') is Arrian's pocket digest of the Discourses, not a separate book by Epictetus.
evidence: this work also was put together by Arrian, who selected from the discourses of Epictetus what he considered to be most useful
author: George Long (1877)
tier: late ancient testimony via 19th c. scholar

claim: Arrian, the student who wrote him down, later became the historian of Alexander the Great.
evidence: an affectionate pupil, Arrian, afterwards the historian of Alexander the Great
author: George Long (1877)

claim: A thief stole his iron lamp. His reply: tomorrow I'll buy a clay one, you only lose what you have.
evidence: Tomorrow, I said, you will find an earthen lamp: for a man only loses that which he has
author: Epictetus
use_in: Recognisable scene reel; Free Minds no

claim: After his death, an admirer is said to have paid 3,000 drachmas for that clay lamp.
evidence: an admirer bought his oil lamp for 3,000 drachmae (Lucian, Remarks to an Illiterate Book-Lover)
author: Lucian
licence: Lucian's Greek is public domain; check the translation's licence before quoting
tier: ancient testimony (2nd c.), not yet checked in Lucian's text
caveat: Read on Wikipedia only. Before use, check Lucian's text (Fowler 1905 translation on Gutenberg/Wikisource) with the discover workflow.

claim: Rufus, asked if Providence still ran the world after the emperor Galba was murdered, said he'd never based that argument on Galba.
evidence: Did I ever incidentally form an argument from Galba that the world is governed by Providence?
author: Epictetus quoting Musonius Rufus
caveat: Needs one line of context: Galba was emperor, killed AD 69.

claim: He told the story of Lateranus who, sentenced by Nero, calmly stretched out his neck a second time after a weak blow.
evidence: he stretched it out again
author: Epictetus
caveat: Violent image: text-only, no illustration (no-faces rule).

claim: Things are split into what is in our power and what is not: the opening line of the Enchiridion.
evidence: Of things some are in our power, and others are not
author: Epictetus

claim: We're upset not by events but by our opinions about them.
evidence: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things
author: Epictetus
caveat: Long's exact words. Do not swap in the popular paraphrase without labelling it Moodius.

claim: His own lameness shows up in his teaching: it limits the leg, not the will.
evidence: Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will
author: Epictetus

claim: Don't wish for events to go your way; want them as they are.
evidence: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are
author: Epictetus

claim: He called a philosopher's school a surgery: you should leave hurting, not pleased.
evidence: The philosopher's school, ye men, is a surgery: you ought not to go out of it with pleasure, but with pain
author: Epictetus

claim: His two-word rule, as reported by a Roman writer: bear and forbear.
evidence: These two words, he said, are a)ne/xou (bear) and a)pe/xou (forbear)
author: Aulus Gellius reporting Favorinus
licence: Public domain translation (Rolfe 1927); Perseus encoding CC BY-SA 4.0, credit Perseus
caveat: Second-hand: Gellius heard it from Favorinus. Greek: anechou, apechou.

claim: Marcus Aurelius thanks his teacher Rusticus for lending him Epictetus's discourses from his own collection.
evidence: I am indebted to him for being acquainted with the discourses of Epictetus, which he communicated to me out of his own collection
author: Marcus Aurelius
use_in: Part 3: from slave to emperor's bookshelf

claim: The founders of cognitive therapy wrote that its philosophical origins go back to the Stoics.
evidence: The philosophical origins of cognitive therapy can be traced back to the Stoic philosophers
source: Beck, Rush, Shaw & Emery, Cognitive Therapy of Depression (Guilford, 1979)
author: Aaron T. Beck et al.
licence: Copyrighted book: one short credited line only
caveat: Checked only through Donald Robertson's quotation. Confirm on p. 8 of the book (Open Library/Internet Archive borrow) before the deep-dive carousel.

claim: US Navy pilot James Stockdale, shot down over Vietnam on 9 Sept 1965, said he told himself as he ejected he was entering 'the world of Epictetus'.
evidence: I'm leaving the world of technology and entering the world of Epictetus.
source: Stockdale, Courage under Fire: Testing Epictetus's Doctrines in a Laboratory of Human Behavior (Hoover Essays 6, 1993)
author: James Bond Stockdale
licence: Copyrighted essay: one short credited line only
caveat: Same essay: a Stanford professor, Philip Rhinelander, gave him the Enchiridion (p. 2); about eight years a prisoner. War image: text-only.

claim: Marcus Aurelius quotes Epictetus: you are a little soul carrying a corpse.
evidence: Thou art a little soul bearing about a corpse, as Epictetus used to say
author: Marcus Aurelius
caveat: Section number is from standard numbering; the word check covers book 4.
